reminder: The terms of a Cauchy sequence come arbitrarily close to each other, all beyond some index.
definition: A [sequence](c:sequence) $(a_n)$ in a [metric space](c:metric-space) $(X,d)$ is Cauchy when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, some $N$ gives $d(a_m,a_n)<\varepsilon$ for all $m,n\ge N$. Every convergent sequence is Cauchy, but a Cauchy sequence can fail to converge when the space has holes.
examples: The sequence $a_n=1/n$ in $\mathbb{R}$ is Cauchy: for $m,n\ge N$ we have $|a_m-a_n|<1/N$.
The decimal truncations $1,\,1.4,\,1.41,\,1.414,\dots$ of $\sqrt2$ form a Cauchy sequence in the [rational numbers](c:rational-number) that has no limit there.
Non-example: The sequence $a_n=n$ in $\mathbb{R}$ is not Cauchy, because $|a_{n+1}-a_n|=1$ for every $n$.

steps: Take a sequence $(a_n)$ in a metric space and its tail filter, generated by the sets $\{a_n:n\ge N\}$.
A filter is Cauchy when it contains sets of arbitrarily small diameter.
The set $\{a_n:n\ge N\}$ has diameter at most $\varepsilon$ exactly when $d(a_m,a_n)\le\varepsilon$ for all $m,n\ge N$.
So the sequence is Cauchy exactly when its tail filter is Cauchy.
links.why: Shows that Cauchy sequences, nets and filters express one idea, which defines completeness in uniform spaces.

reminder: An eigenvector is a nonzero vector that a [linear map](c:linear-map) sends to a scalar multiple of itself.
definition: Let $A:V\to V$ be a [linear map](c:linear-map) of a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ over a field $K$. A vector $v\in V$ is an eigenvector of $A$ when $v\ne0$ and $Av=\lambda v$ for some scalar $\lambda\in K$, the eigenvalue of $v$.
examples: For $A=\operatorname{diag}(2,3)$, the vector $(1,0)$ is an eigenvector with $\lambda=2$.
The function $e^{3x}$ is an eigenvector of the derivative $d/dx$ on smooth functions, with $\lambda=3$.
Non-example: The zero vector satisfies $A0=\lambda0$ for every $\lambda$, so the definition excludes it.
Non-example: The rotation of $\mathbb{R}^2$ by $90^\circ$ has no eigenvector over $\mathbb{R}$, because it turns every nonzero vector off its own line.

steps: Take a nonzero eigenvector $v$ of $A$ with $Av=\lambda v$.
Look at the line $L=\{cv:c\in K\}$ that $v$ spans.
Then $A(cv)=\lambda cv$ lies in $L$, so $A$ maps $L$ into itself.
So $L$ is an invariant subspace, and the eigenvector case adds the condition that $L$ has dimension one.
links.why: Shows that eigenvectors are the one-dimensional invariant subspaces, so a search for invariant subspaces starts with eigenvectors.

reminder: A filtration is a family of sigma-algebras that only grows as time increases.
definition: Let $(\Omega,\mathcal{F})$ be a measurable space and $(I,\le)$ a [partially ordered](c:partial-order) index set, usually the times $\mathbb{N}$ or $[0,\infty)$. A filtration is a family $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t\in I}$ of [sigma-algebras](c:sigma-algebra) contained in $\mathcal{F}$ with $\mathcal{F}_s\subseteq\mathcal{F}_t$ whenever $s\le t$. In algebra, the same word means an increasing family of subobjects, such as subspaces $V_0\subseteq V_1\subseteq\cdots$.
examples: For a process $(X_n)$, the natural filtration $\mathcal{F}_n=\sigma(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ holds the events decided by the first $n$ values.
The coordinate subspaces $0\subset\mathbb{R}^1\subset\mathbb{R}^2\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ form a filtration of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^3$.

Non-example: For independent fair coin tosses $X_1$ and $X_2$, the family $\mathcal{F}_1=\sigma(X_1)$, $\mathcal{F}_2=\sigma(X_2)$ is not a filtration, because $\mathcal{F}_1\not\subseteq\mathcal{F}_2$.

reminder: An irreducible representation is nonzero and has no invariant subspace except zero and the whole space.
definition: A [representation](c:group-representation) $\rho$ of a group $G$ on a vector space $V$ is irreducible when $V\ne0$ and the only $G$-[invariant subspaces](c:invariant-subspace) of $V$ are $0$ and $V$. A [subspace](c:linear-subspace) $W$ is $G$-invariant when $\rho(g)w\in W$ for all $g\in G$ and $w\in W$.
examples: Every one-dimensional representation is irreducible, because its only subspaces are $0$ and the whole space.
The standard representation of $S_3$ on $\{x\in\mathbb{R}^3:x_1+x_2+x_3=0\}$ is irreducible.
The rotation by $90^\circ$ gives an irreducible representation of $\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ but a reducible one on $\mathbb{C}^2$.
Non-example: The permutation representation of $S_3$ on $\mathbb{C}^3$ is not irreducible, because the line spanned by $(1,1,1)$ is invariant.

steps: Take an irreducible representation $\rho:G\to GL(V)$.
It is a representation of $G$ on $V$, so every axiom of a representation holds.
Irreducibility adds the condition $V\ne0$.
It also adds that no invariant subspace lies strictly between $0$ and $V$.
links.why: Shows irreducible representations as the pieces that cannot be split; for a finite group over $\mathbb{C}$, every representation is a sum of them.

reminder: A normed space is a real or complex vector space with a norm that measures the length of vectors.
definition: A normed space is a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ with a [norm](c:norm) $\|\cdot\|:V\to[0,\infty)$. The norm satisfies $\|v\|=0$ only for $v=0$, $\|cv\|=|c|\,\|v\|$ for every scalar $c$, and $\|u+v\|\le\|u\|+\|v\|$.
examples: The space $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $\|x\|=\sqrt{x_1^2+\cdots+x_n^2}$ is a normed space.
The space $C[0,1]$ of continuous functions with $\|f\|=\max_t|f(t)|$ is a normed space.
Non-example: On $\mathbb{R}^2$ the function $p(x,y)=|x|$ is not a norm, because $p(0,1)=0$ for a nonzero vector.

steps: Take a normed space $(V,\|\cdot\|)$ and define $d(u,v)=\|u-v\|$.
Positivity, symmetry and the triangle inequality of $d$ follow from the three norm rules.
So $(V,d)$ is a metric space.
The norm adds that $d$ is invariant under translation and satisfies $d(cu,cv)=|c|\,d(u,v)$.
links.why: Lets you use balls, convergence and completeness in every normed space.

steps: Take an inner product space $V$ with inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and put $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$.
Positive definiteness gives $\|v\|=0$ only for $v=0$, and bilinearity gives $\|cv\|=|c|\,\|v\|$.
The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives the triangle inequality, so $V$ is a normed space.
The converse needs the parallelogram law: a norm comes from an inner product exactly when it holds.
links.why: Shows which normed spaces are inner product spaces, so you can use angles and orthogonality there.

steps: Take a Banach space, a normed space in which every Cauchy sequence converges.
It already has a vector space structure and a norm, so it is a normed space.
A normed space keeps these two structures and does not ask for completeness.
The space of polynomials on $[0,1]$ with the supremum norm is normed but not complete.
links.why: Shows that completeness is the one condition that separates Banach spaces from normed spaces.

reminder: A polynomial ring consists of the polynomials in given variables with coefficients in a ring, with the usual sum and product.
definition: For a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$, the polynomial ring $R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ is the set of finite sums $\sum a_\alpha x_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots x_n^{\alpha_n}$ with $a_\alpha\in R$. Two [polynomials](c:polynomial) add coefficient by coefficient and multiply by distributivity with $x^\alpha x^\beta=x^{\alpha+\beta}$.
examples: The ring $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ contains $3x^2-5x+1$, and the ring $\mathbb{R}[x,y]$ contains $x^2y-y^3$.
An element of the ring is a formal expression, not a function: in $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})[x]$ the polynomial $x^2+x$ is nonzero, although it takes the value $0$ at every point.
Non-example: The ring of [formal power series](c:formal-power-series) $R[[x]]$ is not a polynomial ring, because it allows infinite sums such as $1+x+x^2+\cdots$.

steps: Take $R[x]$ with the sum and product of polynomials.
Addition is coefficientwise, so it is associative and commutative, with zero polynomial and negatives.
Multiplication is associative and commutative because it comes from $R$ and from the rule $x^ax^b=x^{a+b}$.
So $R[x]$ is a commutative ring; the polynomial case adds the free generator $x$ with no relation.
links.why: Lets you use ideals, quotients and every theorem on commutative rings for polynomials.

reminder: A quadratic form is a function on a vector space that is a homogeneous polynomial of degree two in coordinates.
definition: A quadratic form on a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ over a field $K$ is a map $Q:V\to K$ with $Q(cv)=c^2Q(v)$ for all scalars $c$, such that $B(u,v)=Q(u+v)-Q(u)-Q(v)$ is a [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form). In coordinates, $Q$ is a [homogeneous polynomial](c:homogeneous-polynomial) $\sum_{i\le j}a_{ij}x_ix_j$ of degree two.
examples: The function $Q(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is the squared length.
For a symmetric matrix $A$, the function $Q(v)=v^{T}Av$ is a quadratic form.
Non-example: The function $f(x,y)=x^2+y$ is not a quadratic form, because $f(cx,cy)\ne c^2f(x,y)$ in general.

steps: Fix a basis $e_1,\dots,e_n$ of $V$, and let $B(u,v)=Q(u+v)-Q(u)-Q(v)$.
Expanding $Q\left(\sum x_ie_i\right)$ gives $\sum_iQ(e_i)x_i^2+\sum_{i<j}B(e_i,e_j)x_ix_j$.
Every term has degree two in $x_1,\dots,x_n$, so $Q$ is a homogeneous polynomial.
The quadratic case adds that the degree is exactly two and that the polynomial comes from a bilinear form.
links.why: Lets you treat a quadratic form as a polynomial in coordinates and as a bilinear form at the same time.

reminder: A vector field gives each point of a manifold one tangent vector at that point.
definition: A vector field on a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ assigns to each point $p\in M$ a vector $X(p)$ in the [tangent space](c:tangent-space) $T_pM$, a fibre of the [tangent bundle](c:tangent-bundle). It is smooth when the map $p\mapsto X(p)$ is a [smooth map](c:smooth-map) $M\to TM$.
examples: On $\mathbb{R}^2$, the field $X(x,y)=(-y,x)$ turns each point around the origin.
The gradient $\nabla f$ of a smooth function $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a vector field.
Non-example: The constant map $p\mapsto(0,0,1)$ on the sphere $S^2$ is not a vector field of $S^2$, because the vector is not tangent at the north pole.

reminder: A functor $F$ is left adjoint to $G$ when maps $FX\to Y$ correspond naturally to maps $X\to GY$.
definition: Let $F:C\to D$ and $G:D\to C$ be [functors](c:functor) between [categories](c:category). The functor $F$ is left adjoint to $G$, and $G$ is right adjoint to $F$, when there is a bijection $\mathrm{Hom}_D(FX,Y)\cong\mathrm{Hom}_C(X,GY)$ of [hom-sets](c:hom-set) for all objects $X$ of $C$ and $Y$ of $D$, [natural](c:natural-isomorphism) in $X$ and $Y$.
examples: The [free group](c:free-group) functor from sets to groups is left adjoint to the [forgetful functor](c:forgetful-functor): a map from a set $S$ to a group $H$ is the same as a homomorphism from the free group on $S$ to $H$.
For vector spaces, the functor $-\otimes B$ is left adjoint to the functor $\mathrm{Hom}(B,-)$.
Non-example: The forgetful functor from [fields](c:field) to sets has no left adjoint, because that would give an initial field, and fields of different characteristic admit no maps between them.

steps: Take an equivalence $F:C\to D$ with inverse $G$ and natural isomorphisms $\eta:1\to GF$ and $\varepsilon:FG\to1$.
Adjust $\eta$ and $\varepsilon$ so that they satisfy the triangle identities, which gives an adjoint equivalence.
Send $f:FX\to Y$ to $G(f)\circ\eta_X:X\to GY$; this is a natural bijection.
So $F$ is left adjoint to $G$; a general adjunction asks only for natural $\eta$ and $\varepsilon$ with the triangle identities, not for isomorphisms.
links.why: Shows that an equivalence is an adjunction with invertible unit and counit, so adjoint tools apply to it.

steps: Take two posets $P$ and $Q$ as categories with one arrow $x\to y$ when $x\le y$.
Monotone maps $f:P\to Q$ and $g:Q\to P$ are functors between these categories.
Each hom-set has at most one element, so a natural bijection says that $f(x)\le y$ exactly when $x\le g(y)$.
This is exactly the definition of a Galois connection.
links.why: Shows that Galois connections are adjunctions between posets, so results on adjoints cover them.

reminder: A sequence of homomorphisms is exact when the image of each map equals the kernel of the next map.
definition: A sequence $\cdots\to A_{i-1}\xrightarrow{f_{i-1}}A_i\xrightarrow{f_i}A_{i+1}\to\cdots$ of [homomorphisms](c:homomorphism) is exact at $A_i$ when $\operatorname{im}f_{i-1}=\ker f_i$, the [image](c:image) of one map equal to the [kernel](c:kernel-of-a-homomorphism) of the next. It is exact when it is exact at every inner term. In a short exact sequence $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$, the map $A\to B$ is injective, the map $B\to C$ is surjective and the image of $A\to B$ is the kernel of $B\to C$.
examples: The sequence $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\,2\,}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\to0$ is exact: the image of multiplication by $2$ is the kernel of reduction modulo $2$.
For a homomorphism $f:A\to B$ of abelian groups, the sequence $0\to\ker f\to A\to\operatorname{im}f\to0$ is exact.

Non-example: The sequence $\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\,2\,}\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\,3\,}\mathbb{Z}$ is not exact in the middle, because the image is $2\mathbb{Z}$ but the kernel of multiplication by $3$ is $0$.

steps: Take an exact sequence with maps $f_i$, so $\operatorname{im}f_{i-1}=\ker f_i$ at each place.
Then $\operatorname{im}f_{i-1}\subseteq\ker f_i$, which says $f_i\circ f_{i-1}=0$.
So the sequence is a chain complex.
Exactness adds the condition that the homology $\ker f_i/\operatorname{im}f_{i-1}$ vanishes at every place.
links.why: Shows that an exact sequence is a chain complex without homology, so homology measures the failure of exactness.

reminder: A field is a commutative ring in which $0\ne1$ and every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse.
definition: A field is a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $K$ with $0\ne1$ in which every nonzero element $a$ has an inverse $a^{-1}$ with $aa^{-1}=1$. So a field has addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by nonzero elements, with the usual rules.
examples: The [rational numbers](c:rational-number), the real numbers and the [complex numbers](c:complex-number) are fields.
The ring $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ is a field when $p$ is a prime number.
Non-example: The ring $\mathbb{Z}$ is not a field, because $2$ has no inverse in $\mathbb{Z}$.
Non-example: The ring $\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$ is not a field, because $2\cdot3=0$ with $2\ne0$ and $3\ne0$.

steps: Take a field $K$ with its addition and multiplication.
The field axioms already say that $K$ is a commutative ring with identity.
A field adds two conditions: $0\ne1$, and every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse.
So a field is exactly a nonzero commutative ring whose only ideals are $0$ and $K$.
links.why: Lets you use ring tools in a field and shows what a field adds: division.

steps: Take a field $K$.
Every nonzero element of $K$ has an inverse, so $K$ is a division ring.
A field adds that multiplication is commutative.
The quaternions form a division ring with noncommutative multiplication, so this condition is not automatic.
links.why: Separates fields from noncommutative division rings such as the quaternions.

reminder: A random variable is a measurable function from a probability space to the real numbers or another measurable space.
definition: A random variable on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)$, where $P$ is a [probability measure](c:probability-measure) on $\mathcal{F}$, is a [measurable function](c:measurable-function) $X:\Omega\to E$ into a [measurable space](c:measurable-space) $(E,\mathcal{E})$, often $\mathbb{R}$ with its Borel sets. Measurable means $X^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal{F}$ for every $B\in\mathcal{E}$, so $P(X\in B)$ is defined.
examples: The number of heads in three fair coin tosses is a random variable on $\Omega=\{H,T\}^3$.
The indicator $1_A$ of an event $A\in\mathcal{F}$ is a random variable.
The identity map $X(\omega)=\omega$ on $[0,1]$ with Lebesgue measure is a uniform random variable.
Non-example: The indicator of a nonmeasurable subset $A\subseteq[0,1]$, such as a Vitali set, is not a random variable, because $\{X=1\}=A$ is not in $\mathcal{F}$.

steps: Take a random variable $X:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)$.
By definition, $X^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal{F}$ for every Borel set $B$.
So $X$ is a measurable function from $(\Omega,\mathcal{F})$ to $\mathbb{R}$.
The probabilistic case adds that $\mathcal{F}$ carries a probability measure $P$, which gives $X$ its distribution.
links.why: Lets you use all results on measurable functions, such as closure under sums and limits, for random variables.

reminder: A simply connected space is path-connected, and every loop in it shrinks continuously to a point.
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is simply connected when it is [path-connected](c:path-connected-space) and its [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group) is trivial. Equivalently, every loop in $X$ can be continuously shrunk to a point.
examples: The space $\mathbb{R}^n$ and each convex subset of it are simply connected: the straight-line homotopy shrinks every loop.
The sphere $S^n$ is simply connected for $n\ge2$.
Non-example: The circle $S^1$ is path-connected but not simply connected, because its fundamental group is $\mathbb{Z}$ and a loop that winds once cannot shrink.

steps: Take a simply connected space $X$.
By definition, any two points of $X$ are joined by a path, so $X$ is path-connected.
Simply connected adds that the fundamental group $\pi_1(X,x)$ is trivial at each base point.
The circle is path-connected with $\pi_1=\mathbb{Z}$, so the added condition is real.
links.why: Shows exactly what simple connectivity adds to path-connectedness: loops carry no winding information.

steps: Take a contractible space $X$ with a homotopy $H:X\times[0,1]\to X$ from the identity to a constant map.
For each $x$, the path $t\mapsto H(x,t)$ joins $x$ to the constant point, so $X$ is path-connected.
A loop $\gamma$ shrinks through the loops $H(\gamma(s),t)$, so every loop is homotopic to a constant loop.
So $X$ is simply connected; the converse fails, because the sphere $S^2$ is simply connected but not contractible.
links.why: Gives a quick test: every contractible space is simply connected, while the converse needs more tools.

reminder: A chain is an element of a chain complex or, in an ordered set, a subset whose elements are pairwise comparable.
definition: In order theory, a chain in a [partially ordered set](c:partial-order) is a subset $C$ such that any two elements $x,y\in C$ satisfy $x\le y$ or $y\le x$. In homological algebra, an $n$-chain is an element of the group $C_n$ of a [chain complex](c:chain-complex) $(C_\bullet,\partial)$.
examples: In the divisibility order on $\mathbb{N}$, the set $\{1,2,4,8\}$ is a chain.
Every subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is a chain for the usual order $\le$.
In singular homology, a $2$-chain is a formal sum of singular $2$-simplices, an element of $C_2$.
Non-example: In the divisibility order on $\mathbb{N}$, the set $\{2,3\}$ is not a chain, because neither $2\mid3$ nor $3\mid2$.

reminder: A CW complex is a space built by attaching cells of increasing dimension along their boundaries.
definition: A CW complex is a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X=\bigcup_nX^n$ in which $X^0$ is a discrete set and each $X^n$ is the [quotient](c:quotient-space) of the [disjoint union](c:disjoint-union) of $X^{n-1}$ and copies of the [unit ball](c:unit-ball) $D^n$, obtained by gluing each boundary sphere $\partial D^n$ to $X^{n-1}$ along a map. A subset of $X$ is closed exactly when it meets every closed cell in a closed set.
examples: The sphere $S^n$ has one $0$-cell and one $n$-cell, attached by the constant map.
The torus has one $0$-cell, two $1$-cells and one $2$-cell.
Non-example: The Cantor set is not a CW complex, because cells of positive dimension are connected, so a CW structure on it would be discrete, and the Cantor set is not discrete.

steps: Take a simplicial complex $K$ and its geometric realization $|K|$.
Each closed $n$-simplex is homeomorphic to the ball $D^n$, and its boundary lies in the $(n-1)$-skeleton.
Attach the simplices in order of dimension; the result has one cell for each simplex.
So $|K|$ is a CW complex; a general CW complex lets cells attach along arbitrary maps, not only simplicial ones.
links.why: Shows that every simplicial complex is a CW complex, so cellular tools apply with far fewer cells.

reminder: An entire function is a function that is holomorphic on the whole complex plane.
definition: An entire function is a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) $f:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ defined on the whole set of [complex numbers](c:complex-number). Equivalently, its [Taylor series](c:taylor-series) at $0$ converges to $f(z)$ for every $z$.
examples: Every polynomial, such as $z^3-2z+1$, is entire.
The functions $e^z$, $\sin z$ and $\cos z$ are entire.
Non-example: The function $1/z$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$ but is not entire, because it has a pole at $0$.
Non-example: The function $\bar z$ is defined on all of $\mathbb{C}$ but is not holomorphic at any point.

steps: Take an entire function $f$.
It is holomorphic at every point of $\mathbb{C}$, so it is holomorphic on the open set $\mathbb{C}$.
The entire case adds that the domain of holomorphy is the whole plane, with no singular point.
This extra condition makes Liouville-type results possible: a bounded entire function is constant.
links.why: Shows that entire functions are holomorphic functions without singularities, which gives them global tools.

steps: Take a polynomial $p(z)=\sum_{k\le n}a_kz^k$ with complex coefficients.
It is complex differentiable at each $z$, with $p'(z)=\sum_{k\ge1}ka_kz^{k-1}$.
So $p$ is holomorphic on all of $\mathbb{C}$, hence entire.
The functions $e^z$ and $\sin z$ are entire but not polynomials, so the converse fails.
links.why: Places polynomials as the entire functions with finitely many Taylor terms, which guides what you can prove for them.

reminder: The Fourier transform sends a function to its integrals against complex exponentials, one for each frequency.
definition: The Fourier transform of an [integrable function](c:integrable-function) $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the function $\hat f(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)\,e^{-2\pi i\,x\cdot\xi}\,dx$ of the frequency $\xi$. It is the [integral](c:integral) of $f$ against the complex [exponential](c:exponential-function) of frequency $\xi$.
examples: The Gaussian $e^{-\pi x^2}$ on $\mathbb{R}$ equals its own Fourier transform.
The indicator of $[-\tfrac12,\tfrac12]$ has the Fourier transform $\sin(\pi\xi)/(\pi\xi)$.
Non-example: The constant function $1$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is not integrable, so the integral does not define $\hat1$ as a function; as a distribution, $\hat1$ is the Dirac mass at $0$.

steps: Take an integrable function $f$ and view it as the distribution $\varphi\mapsto\int f\varphi$.
The transform of a distribution $T$ is defined by $\langle\hat T,\varphi\rangle=\langle T,\hat\varphi\rangle$.
Fubini's theorem gives $\int\hat f\varphi=\int f\hat\varphi$ for each test function $\varphi$.
So the distribution transform of $f$ is the function $\hat f$; the distribution version also covers $1$ and the Dirac mass.
links.why: Shows the integral formula as the function case of the Fourier transform, which extends to objects such as the Dirac mass.

reminder: In a Hausdorff space, any two distinct points have disjoint open neighborhoods.
definition:
A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is Hausdorff when, for all points $x
e y$, there are [open sets](c:open-set) $U
i x$ and $V
i y$ with $U\cap V=\varnothing$.
examples: Every metric space is Hausdorff: the balls of radius $d(x,y)/2$ around $x$ and $y$ are disjoint.
The space $\mathbb{R}^n$ with its usual topology is Hausdorff.
Non-example: An infinite set with the cofinite topology is not Hausdorff, because any two nonempty open sets meet.
Non-example: The line with two origins is not Hausdorff, because the two origins have no disjoint open neighborhoods.

steps: Take a Hausdorff space $X$ and a point $x$.

For each $y
e x$, choose disjoint open sets $U_y
i y$ and $V
i x$, so $U_y$ misses $x$.
Then $X\setminus\{x\}=\bigcup_yU_y$ is open, so $\{x\}$ is closed and $X$ is a T1 space.
The Hausdorff case adds that two points are separated by disjoint open sets, not only each from the other.
links.why: Shows that Hausdorff is a stronger separation axiom than T1, so points are closed in every Hausdorff space.

steps: Take a metric space $(X,d)$ with its metric topology and points $x\ne y$.
Put $r=d(x,y)/2>0$ and take the open balls $B(x,r)$ and $B(y,r)$.
A point $z$ in both balls would give $d(x,y)\le d(x,z)+d(z,y)<2r=d(x,y)$, which is absurd.
So the balls are disjoint open sets, and the metric topology is Hausdorff.
links.why: Shows that every metric space is a Hausdorff space, so limits of sequences are unique there.

steps: Take a compact Hausdorff space $X$.
It is a space in which distinct points have disjoint open neighborhoods, so it is Hausdorff.
Compactness is the added condition: every open cover of $X$ has a finite subcover.
Compact Hausdorff spaces are also normal, a strength that general Hausdorff spaces lack.
links.why: Shows what compactness adds to the Hausdorff property, which is the setting of many classical theorems.

reminder: A monotone function keeps the order: if $x\le y$, then $f(x)\le f(y)$.
definition: A [function](c:function) $f:P\to Q$ between [partially ordered sets](c:partial-order) is monotone, or increasing, when $x\le y$ implies $f(x)\le f(y)$ for all $x,y\in P$. It is antitone, or decreasing, when $x\le y$ implies $f(y)\le f(x)$.
examples: The function $x\mapsto x^3$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is monotone.
The size map $A\mapsto|A|$ from the finite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$, ordered by inclusion, to $\mathbb{N}$ is monotone.
The floor function $\lfloor x\rfloor$ is monotone but not strictly monotone.
Non-example: The function $x\mapsto x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is neither monotone nor antitone, because $-2\le1$ gives $4>1$ and $1\le2$ gives $1<4$.

steps: Take a real sequence $(a_n)$ as a function $a:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}$.
Give $\mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbb{R}$ their usual orders.
The sequence is increasing exactly when $m\le n$ implies $a_m\le a_n$.
So a monotone sequence is a monotone function whose domain is $\mathbb{N}$.
links.why: Lets you carry results on monotone sequences, such as the monotone convergence theorem, to monotone functions.

reminder: A unitary operator is a bounded linear operator on a Hilbert space whose adjoint is its inverse.
definition: A [bounded operator](c:bounded-operator) $U$ on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ is unitary when $U^*U=UU^*=I$, where $U^*$ is the [adjoint operator](c:adjoint-operator) of $U$. Equivalently, $U$ is a surjective linear map that preserves the inner product.
examples: Every complex matrix $Q$ with $Q^*Q=I$ is a unitary operator on $\mathbb{C}^n$, for example a rotation matrix.
Multiplication by $e^{i\theta}$ on $\mathbb{C}$ is a unitary operator.
The Fourier transform on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$, with the factor $2\pi$ in the exponent, is a unitary operator.
Non-example: The shift $S(x_1,x_2,\dots)=(0,x_1,x_2,\dots)$ on $\ell^2$ has $S^*S=I$ but $SS^*\ne I$, so it is not unitary; it is not surjective.

steps: Take a unitary operator $U$ on $H$.
Then $\langle Ux,Uy\rangle=\langle x,U^*Uy\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle$ for all $x,y$.
So $U$ preserves inner products and norms, and it is a linear isometry.
The condition $UU^*=I$ adds that $U$ is surjective.
links.why: Shows that unitary operators are the isometries that are also onto, so they are the symmetries of a Hilbert space.

reminder: An algebraic number is a complex number that is a root of a nonzero polynomial with rational coefficients.
definition: A [complex number](c:complex-number) $\alpha$ is algebraic when it is a [root](c:root-of-a-polynomial) of a nonzero [polynomial](c:polynomial) with [rational](c:rational-number) coefficients. A complex number that is not algebraic is transcendental.
examples: The number $\sqrt2$ is algebraic: it is a root of $x^2-2$.
Every rational number $p/q$ is algebraic: it is a root of $qx-p$.
The number $i$ is algebraic: it is a root of $x^2+1$.
Non-example: The numbers $\pi$ and $e$ are not algebraic, because no nonzero polynomial with rational coefficients vanishes at them.

steps: Take the field extension $\mathbb{C}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$.
An element $\alpha\in\mathbb{C}$ is algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$ when some nonzero polynomial in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$ vanishes at $\alpha$.
That is the definition of an algebraic number.
So the general notion fixes the base field $\mathbb{Q}$ and the larger field $\mathbb{C}$.
links.why: Lets you use the theory of algebraic elements, such as minimal polynomials, for algebraic numbers.

steps: Take an algebraic integer $\alpha$, a root of a monic polynomial in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.
That polynomial has rational coefficients and is nonzero, because it is monic.
So $\alpha$ is an algebraic number.
The algebraic integers are the algebraic numbers whose minimal polynomial over $\mathbb{Q}$ has integer coefficients.
links.why: Shows that algebraic integers form a special class inside the algebraic numbers, so you can test integrality through the minimal polynomial.

reminder: The angle between two nonzero vectors is the arccosine of their inner product divided by the product of their lengths.
definition: For nonzero vectors $u,v$ in a real [inner product space](c:inner-product-space) such as a [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space), the angle is $\theta=\arccos\dfrac{\langle u,v\rangle}{\|u\|\,\|v\|}\in[0,\pi]$, where $\|u\|$ is the [norm](c:norm) of $u$. For two rays from a common point, it is the angle between their direction vectors.
examples: The vectors $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ have the angle $\pi/4$.
Perpendicular vectors have the angle $\pi/2$, because $\langle u,v\rangle=0$.
The vectors $u$ and $-u$ have the angle $\pi$.
Non-example: The zero vector has no angle with any vector, because the quotient divides by $\|0\|=0$.

reminder: A measure is finite when the whole space has finite measure.
definition: A [measure](c:measure) $\mu$ on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal{A})$ is finite when $\mu(X)<\infty$. Then every measurable set has finite measure, because $\mu(A)\le\mu(X)$ for $A\in\mathcal{A}$.
examples: Every probability measure is finite, with $\mu(X)=1$.
The restriction of [Lebesgue measure](c:lebesgue-measure) to $[0,1]$ is finite, with total mass $1$.
Non-example: Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}$ is not finite, because $\lambda(\mathbb{R})=\infty$.
Non-example: Counting measure on $\mathbb{N}$ is not finite, because $\mu(\mathbb{N})=\infty$.

steps: Take a probability measure $P$, so $P(X)=1$.
Then $P(X)<\infty$, so $P$ is a finite measure.
Conversely, a finite measure $\mu$ with $\mu(X)>0$ gives the probability measure $\mu/\mu(X)$.
So finite measures are the probability measures up to a positive constant.
links.why: Lets you turn every nonzero finite measure into a probability measure by normalizing.

steps: Take a finite measure $\mu$ on $X$.
The single set $X$ has $\mu(X)<\infty$ and covers $X$.
So $X$ is a countable union of sets of finite measure, and $\mu$ is sigma-finite.
Sigma-finite is weaker: Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}$ is sigma-finite but not finite.
links.why: Shows that results proved for sigma-finite measures, such as Fubini's theorem, apply to finite measures.

reminder: A Kähler manifold is a Hermitian manifold whose fundamental two-form is closed.
definition: A Kähler manifold is a [Hermitian manifold](c:hermitian-manifold) $(M,J,g)$ whose fundamental [2-form](c:differential-form) $\omega(u,v)=g(Ju,v)$ is closed, $d\omega=0$. Then $\omega$ is a [symplectic form](c:symplectic-form), and the [complex](c:complex-manifold) and [Riemannian](c:riemannian-manifold) structures agree with it.
examples: The space $\mathbb{C}^n$ with the standard Hermitian metric is Kähler.
Complex projective space $\mathbb{CP}^n$ with the Fubini-Study metric is Kähler, and so is every complex submanifold of it.
Every Riemann surface with any Hermitian metric is Kähler, because every 2-form on a surface is closed.

Non-example: The Hopf surface $S^1\times S^3$ is a complex manifold with Hermitian metrics but has no Kähler metric: $H^2(S^1\times S^3;\mathbb{R})=0$ makes a closed $\omega$ exact, which contradicts $\int\omega^2>0$.

steps: Take a Kähler manifold $(M,J,g)$.
By definition, $J$ is a complex structure and $g$ is a Riemannian metric with $g(Ju,Jv)=g(u,v)$, so $M$ is Hermitian.
The Kähler case adds the condition $d\omega=0$ on the fundamental form.
This condition is equivalent to $\nabla J=0$ for the Levi-Civita connection of $g$.
links.why: Shows that Kähler manifolds are Hermitian manifolds with extra rigidity, which gives them Hodge theory.

steps: Take a Kähler manifold $(M,J,g)$ with fundamental form $\omega$.
The form $\omega$ is closed, and it is nondegenerate because $g$ is positive definite and $J$ is invertible.
So $(M,\omega)$ is a symplectic manifold.
The Kähler case adds a complex structure $J$ that is compatible with $\omega$ and $g$.
links.why: Shows that Kähler manifolds carry symplectic geometry and complex geometry at once.

reminder: Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the translation-invariant measure that gives the unit cube volume one.
definition: The Lebesgue measure $\lambda$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the [measure](c:measure) on the [Borel sets](c:borel-set) that is invariant under translations and gives the [unit cube](c:cube) $[0,1]^n$ the value $1$, completed to include all subsets of null sets. It gives each box $\prod_i[a_i,b_i]$ the volume $\prod_i(b_i-a_i)$ in [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space).
examples: On $\mathbb{R}$, the interval $[a,b]$ has $\lambda([a,b])=b-a$.
Every countable set, such as $\mathbb{Q}$, has Lebesgue measure $0$.
The unit disk in $\mathbb{R}^2$ has Lebesgue measure $\pi$.
Non-example: Counting measure on $\mathbb{R}$ is translation invariant but gives $[0,1]$ infinite measure, so it is not Lebesgue measure.

steps: Take $\lambda$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with its Lebesgue sigma-algebra.
It is nonnegative, gives the empty set measure $0$ and is countably additive.
So $(\mathbb{R}^n,\lambda)$ is a measure space.
The added conditions are translation invariance and $\lambda([0,1]^n)=1$, which fix $\lambda$ uniquely on the Borel sets.
links.why: Shows that Lebesgue measure is one measure with extra symmetry, so general measure theory applies to it.

reminder: A Lie group is a group and a smooth manifold in which multiplication and inversion are smooth maps.
definition: A Lie group is a [group](c:group) $G$ that is also a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) such that multiplication $G\times G\to G$ and inversion $G\to G$ are [smooth maps](c:smooth-map).
examples: The vector space $\mathbb{R}^n$ with addition and the circle group $S^1\subset\mathbb{C}^\times$ are Lie groups.
The general linear group $GL_n(\mathbb{R})$ is a Lie group: it is an open subset of the space of matrices.
Non-example: The sphere $S^2$ is a smooth manifold but has no Lie group structure, because a Lie group has a nowhere-zero vector field and $S^2$ has none.

steps: Take a Lie group $G$.
Smooth maps are continuous, so multiplication and inversion are continuous.
So $G$ is a topological group.
The Lie case adds a smooth structure for which the group operations are smooth.
links.why: Lets you use topological group tools, such as Haar measure, for Lie groups.

steps: Take a Lie group $G$ that is compact as a topological space.
It already satisfies the Lie group axioms, so it is a compact Lie group.
Compactness is the only added condition.
It gives a finite Haar measure and makes every finite-dimensional representation a sum of irreducible ones.
links.why: Shows what compactness adds to a Lie group: averaging works, so representation theory is simple.

reminder: An orthonormal basis is a set of mutually orthogonal unit vectors whose span is dense in the space.
definition: An orthonormal basis of an [inner product space](c:inner-product-space) $H$ is a set $\{e_i\}$ of unit vectors with $\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=0$ for $i\ne j$, so the vectors are mutually [orthogonal](c:orthogonality), whose [span](c:span) is [dense](c:dense-set) in $H$. In finite dimension, dense means that the span is all of $H$.
examples: The standard vectors $e_1,\dots,e_n$ form an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
The functions $e^{inx}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ with $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ form an orthonormal basis of $L^2[-\pi,\pi]$.
Non-example: The vectors $e_2,e_3,\dots$ of $\ell^2$ are orthonormal but not a basis, because their span misses $e_1$ and is not dense.

steps: Take an orthonormal basis $\{e_i\}$.
Its vectors are unit vectors and mutually orthogonal, so it is an orthonormal set.
The added condition is that the span is dense.
In a Hilbert space, this condition forces the set to be maximal: a vector orthogonal to every $e_i$ is zero.
links.why: Shows that a basis is an orthonormal set that cannot grow, which gives expansions $x=\sum\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$.

reminder: A permutation of a set is a bijection from the set to itself.
definition: A permutation of a [set](c:set) $X$ is a [bijection](c:bijection) $\sigma:X\to X$ from $X$ to itself. For a finite set, it rearranges the elements of $X$, and the composition of two permutations is again a permutation.
examples: The swap of $1$ and $2$ is a permutation of $\{1,2,3\}$.
The cyclic shift $i\mapsto i+1$ modulo $n$ is a permutation of $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$.
A set with $n$ elements has exactly $n!$ permutations.
Non-example: The map $1\mapsto2$, $2\mapsto2$, $3\mapsto1$ is not a permutation of $\{1,2,3\}$, because it is not injective.

steps: Take a permutation $\sigma$ of $X$.
By definition, $\sigma:X\to X$ is a bijection.
So $\sigma$ is a bijection whose domain and codomain are the same set.
This shared set lets permutations compose with each other and form the symmetric group.
links.why: Lets you use bijection facts, such as the existence of an inverse, for every permutation.

reminder: The cardinal number of a set is its size: two sets have the same cardinal exactly when a bijection joins them.
definition: The cardinal number $|A|$ of a [set](c:set) $A$ measures its size: $|A|=|B|$ exactly when a [bijection](c:bijection) $A\to B$ exists, and $|A|\le|B|$ exactly when an injective map $A\to B$ exists. For a finite set, $|A|$ is the number of its elements.
examples: The set $\{a,b,c\}$ has $|\{a,b,c\}|=3$.
The sets $\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$ all have the cardinal number $\aleph_0$, because bijections exist between them.
The set $\mathbb{R}$ has the cardinal number $2^{\aleph_0}$, which is larger than $\aleph_0$ by Cantor's diagonal argument.
Non-example: The symbol $\infty$ is not one cardinal number: $\mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbb{R}$ are both infinite, but $|\mathbb{N}|<|\mathbb{R}|$.

steps: Take a natural number $n$ and the set $\{1,\dots,n\}$.
Its cardinal number is $n$, and two finite sets have the same cardinal exactly when they have the same count.
So the natural numbers are the cardinal numbers of finite sets.
Cardinal numbers add infinite sizes such as $\aleph_0$.
links.why: Shows that counting extends to infinite sets, so you can compare sizes of infinite sets by bijections.

reminder: The conditional expectation of $X$ given a sigma-algebra $\mathcal{G}$ is the $\mathcal{G}$-measurable variable with the same average as $X$ on every event of $\mathcal{G}$.
definition: Let $X$ be an integrable [random variable](c:random-variable) on $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)$ and $\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{F}$ a [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra). The conditional expectation $E[X\mid\mathcal{G}]$ is the $\mathcal{G}$-measurable random variable $Y$ with $E[Y\,1_A]=E[X\,1_A]$ for every $A\in\mathcal{G}$, unique up to almost sure equality. Here $E$ is the [expected value](c:expected-value).
examples: If $\mathcal{G}=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$, then $E[X\mid\mathcal{G}]$ is the constant $E[X]$.
If $X$ is $\mathcal{G}$-measurable, then $E[X\mid\mathcal{G}]=X$.
If $\mathcal{G}$ is generated by a finite partition, then $E[X\mid\mathcal{G}]$ equals the average of $X$ over each block of the partition.
Non-example: For a nonconstant $X$ and $\mathcal{G}=\sigma(X)$, the constant $E[X]$ is not $E[X\mid\mathcal{G}]$, because the identity fails for $A=\{X>E[X]\}$.

steps: Take the trivial sigma-algebra $\mathcal{G}=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$.
A $\mathcal{G}$-measurable random variable $Y$ is constant.
The condition $E[Y\,1_\Omega]=E[X\,1_\Omega]$ forces $Y=E[X]$.
So $E[X\mid\mathcal{G}]$ is the constant $E[X]$, and the plain expected value is the special case.
links.why: Shows that the plain expected value is a conditional expectation given no information.

steps: Take an event $A$ and a sub-sigma-algebra $\mathcal{G}$.
The indicator $1_A$ is an integrable random variable.
Define $P(A\mid\mathcal{G})=E[1_A\mid\mathcal{G}]$, a $\mathcal{G}$-measurable random variable.
For $\mathcal{G}=\{\varnothing,B,B^c,\Omega\}$ with $P(B)>0$, it equals $P(A\mid B)$ on $B$, the elementary conditional probability.
links.why: Shows that conditional probability given a sigma-algebra is a conditional expectation of an indicator.

reminder: Random variables are independent when the probability that all land in given sets equals the product of the separate probabilities.
definition: [Random variables](c:random-variable) $X_1,\dots,X_n$ on one probability space are independent when $P(X_1\in B_1,\dots,X_n\in B_n)=\prod_iP(X_i\in B_i)$ for all [Borel sets](c:borel-set) $B_1,\dots,B_n$. An infinite family is independent when every finite subfamily is. This is the [independence](c:independence) of the [sigma-algebras](c:sigma-algebra) $\sigma(X_i)$.
examples: The results of two tosses of a fair coin are independent random variables.
The two coordinates of a point chosen uniformly from $[0,1]^2$ are independent.
A random variable and a constant are always independent.
Non-example: If $X$ is uniform on $\{-1,0,1\}$, then $X$ and $X^2$ are uncorrelated but not independent, because $P(X=1,X^2=1)=1/3$ while $P(X=1)P(X^2=1)=2/9$.

steps: Take independent random variables $X$ and $Y$ with the generated sigma-algebras $\sigma(X)$ and $\sigma(Y)$.
Every event of $\sigma(X)$ has the form $\{X\in B\}$ for a Borel set $B$, and likewise for $Y$.
The product rule for all such sets says $P(A\cap C)=P(A)P(C)$ for $A\in\sigma(X)$ and $C\in\sigma(Y)$.
So the sigma-algebras are independent; independence of random variables is independence of the sigma-algebras they generate.
links.why: Lets you use independence of events and sigma-algebras, such as the product rule, for random variables.

reminder: A linear map is a function between vector spaces that preserves addition and scalar multiplication.
definition: A [function](c:function) $T:V\to W$ between [vector spaces](c:vector-space) over the same field is linear when $T(u+v)=T(u)+T(v)$ and $T(cv)=cT(v)$ for all vectors $u,v$ and all scalars $c$.
examples: For a matrix $A$, the function $v\mapsto Av$ is a linear map.
Differentiation $f\mapsto f'$ is a linear map on the space of smooth functions.
Non-example: The function $x\mapsto x+1$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is not linear, because $T(0)=1\ne0$.

steps: Take the vector spaces $V$ and $W$ as abelian groups with a scalar multiplication.
A linear map preserves addition, so it is a group homomorphism of $(V,+)$ to $(W,+)$.
It also preserves scalar multiplication, so it is a homomorphism of vector spaces.
The condition added to a group homomorphism is $T(cv)=cT(v)$ for every scalar $c$.
links.why: Lets you use kernels, images and isomorphism theorems for linear maps.

steps: Take a linear functional $f:V\to K$ on a vector space $V$ over the field $K$.
The field $K$ is a vector space over itself.
So $f$ is a linear map from $V$ to the vector space $K$.
A linear map allows any vector space as target, not only the scalars.
links.why: Shows that linear functionals are the linear maps into the scalars, which leads to the dual space.

reminder: A normal subgroup is a subgroup that conjugation by any group element maps to itself.
definition: A [subgroup](c:subgroup) $N$ of a [group](c:group) $G$ is normal when $gNg^{-1}=N$ for every $g\in G$, so $N$ holds every [conjugate](c:conjugation) $gng^{-1}$ of each of its elements $n$. Then the cosets of $N$ form a group $G/N$.
examples: Every subgroup of an abelian group is normal.
The alternating group $A_n$ is a normal subgroup of the symmetric group $S_n$, because it is the kernel of the sign homomorphism.
Non-example: The subgroup $\langle(1\,2)\rangle$ of $S_3$ is not normal, because conjugation by $(1\,3)$ gives $\langle(2\,3)\rangle$.

steps: Take a normal subgroup $N$ of $G$.
It is a subgroup by definition.
Normality adds that $gNg^{-1}\subseteq N$ for all $g\in G$.
This condition makes the cosets of $N$ multiply, so $G/N$ is a group.
links.why: Shows that normal subgroups are the subgroups that allow quotient groups.

steps: Take a homomorphism $f:G\to H$ and put $N=\ker f$.
For $n\in N$ and $g\in G$, we get $f(gng^{-1})=f(g)f(n)f(g)^{-1}=e$.
So $gng^{-1}\in N$, and $N$ is a normal subgroup.
Conversely, every normal subgroup $N$ is the kernel of the quotient map $G\to G/N$.
links.why: Lets you prove that a subgroup is normal by showing that it is a kernel.

reminder: A partial order is a relation that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive.
definition: A partial order on a [set](c:set) $P$ is a [relation](c:relation) $\le$ on $P$ with three properties: $x\le x$ for all $x$ (reflexive), $x\le y$ and $y\le x$ imply $x=y$ (antisymmetric), and $x\le y$ and $y\le z$ imply $x\le z$ (transitive). Two elements can be incomparable.
examples: The usual order $\le$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is a partial order.
Inclusion $\subseteq$ on the subsets of a set is a partial order.
Divisibility on the positive integers is a partial order.
Non-example: Divisibility on $\mathbb{Z}$ is not antisymmetric, because $2\mid-2$ and $-2\mid2$ but $2\ne-2$.

steps: Take a total order $\le$ on $X$.
A total order is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive by definition, so $\le$ is a partial order.
A total order adds that any two elements $x,y$ satisfy $x\le y$ or $y\le x$.
Inclusion on the subsets of $\{1,2\}$ shows that this condition is not automatic: $\{1\}$ and $\{2\}$ are incomparable.
links.why: Shows that a partial order drops comparability, which lets you order sets, divisors and sigma-algebras.

steps: Take a partial order $\le$ on $P$.
It is reflexive and transitive, so it is a preorder.
Antisymmetry is the added condition.
It makes the order identify equal elements: $x\le y$ and $y\le x$ give $x=y$.
links.why: Shows that a partial order is a preorder without distinct equivalent elements.

reminder: A homeomorphism is a continuous bijection between topological spaces whose inverse is also continuous.
definition: A homeomorphism is a [bijection](c:bijection) $f:X\to Y$ between [topological spaces](c:topological-space) such that both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are [continuous](c:continuous-function). Two spaces with a homeomorphism between them are homeomorphic and have the same topological properties.
examples: The map $x\mapsto x/(1+|x|)$ is a homeomorphism from $\mathbb{R}$ to $(-1,1)$.
Stereographic projection is a homeomorphism from the sphere $S^2$ minus the north pole to $\mathbb{R}^2$.
Non-example: The map $[0,2\pi)\to S^1$, $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$ is a continuous bijection, but its inverse is not continuous at $(1,0)$.

steps: Take the category of topological spaces with the continuous maps as arrows.
An isomorphism in this category is a continuous map $f$ with a continuous two-sided inverse $g$.
The map $f$ is then a bijection, and $g=f^{-1}$.
So an isomorphism of topological spaces is exactly a homeomorphism.
links.why: Shows that a homeomorphism is the notion of sameness for topological spaces, as isomorphism is for groups.

reminder: Every natural number is $0$ or arises from $0$ by adding $1$ finitely many times.
definition: The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,2,\dots\}$ form the set that contains [zero](c:zero) and is closed under the [successor](c:successor) map $n\mapsto n+1$, where $0$ is not a successor and different numbers have different successors. Induction holds: a set that contains $0$ and contains $n+1$ whenever it contains $n$ is all of $\mathbb{N}$.
examples: The numbers $0$, $7$ and $2026$ are natural numbers.
The number of elements of a finite set is a natural number.
Non-example: The numbers $-1$ and $1/2$ are not natural numbers, because neither is $0$ and neither is the successor of a natural number.

steps: Build the integers from pairs $(a,b)$ of natural numbers that stand for $a-b$.
Identify $(a,b)$ with $(c,d)$ when $a+d=b+c$.
Send each natural number $n$ to the class of $(n,0)$; this map is injective and keeps sums and products.
So $\mathbb{N}$ sits inside the integers as the numbers $\ge0$, and the integers add additive inverses.
links.why: Shows that natural numbers are the nonnegative integers, so integer arithmetic extends natural arithmetic.

reminder: A sigma-algebra is a collection of subsets of a set that contains the set and is closed under complements and countable unions.
definition: A sigma-algebra on a [set](c:set) $X$ is a collection $\mathcal{A}$ of subsets of $X$, that is, a subset of the [power set](c:power-set) of $X$, with $X\in\mathcal{A}$, such that the [complement](c:complement) of each member is a member and every [countable](c:countable-set) union of members is a member.
examples: The power set of $X$ and the trivial collection $\{\varnothing,X\}$ are sigma-algebras on $X$.
The Borel sets of $\mathbb{R}$ form a sigma-algebra.
The countable and co-countable subsets of an uncountable set form a sigma-algebra.
Non-example: The finite and cofinite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ are not a sigma-algebra, because the union of the singletons $\{2n\}$ is neither finite nor cofinite.

steps: Take a sigma-algebra $\mathcal{A}$ on $X$.
A finite union $A_1\cup\dots\cup A_n$ is a countable union after repeating $A_n$.
So $\mathcal{A}$ is closed under complements and finite unions, and it is an algebra of sets.
A sigma-algebra adds closure under countable unions, which countable additivity of a measure needs.
links.why: Shows that a sigma-algebra is an algebra of sets that supports limits, so measures can pass to limits of sets.

reminder: A ball in a metric space is the set of points whose distance from the centre is below, or at most, the radius.
definition: In a [metric space](c:metric-space) $(X,d)$, the open ball with centre $x$ and radius $r>0$ is $B(x,r)=\{y\in X:d(x,y)<r\}$. The closed ball is $\bar B(x,r)=\{y\in X:d(x,y)\le r\}$.
examples: In $\mathbb{R}$, the open ball $B(x,r)$ is the interval $(x-r,x+r)$.
In $\mathbb{R}^2$, a Euclidean ball is a disk, and a ball for the metric $\max(|\Delta x|,|\Delta y|)$ is a square.
In a discrete metric space, the open ball $B(x,1)$ is the single point $\{x\}$.
Non-example: The strip $\{(x,y):|x|<1\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is not a ball, because it is unbounded and every ball has diameter at most $2r$.

steps: Take an open ball $B(x,r)$ and a point $y$ in it.
Put $s=r-d(x,y)$, which is positive because $y$ lies in the ball.
If $d(y,z)<s$, the triangle inequality gives $d(x,z)<r$, so $B(y,s)\subseteq B(x,r)$.
Every point of the ball has a smaller ball around it inside the ball, so the open ball is an open set.
links.why: Shows that open balls are open sets, so they form a base for the metric topology.

reminder: Brownian motion is a continuous random path from $0$ with independent normal increments whose variance equals the elapsed time.
definition: Brownian motion is a [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) $(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ with $B_0=0$, [continuous](c:continuous-function) paths and [independent increments](c:independent-increments). For $s<t$, the increment $B_t-B_s$ has the [normal distribution](c:normal-distribution) with mean $0$ and variance $t-s$.
examples: The process $B_t$ with $\operatorname{Var}(B_t)=t$ models the position of a particle that diffuses on a line.
For $c>0$, the rescaled process $\tfrac1cB_{c^2t}$ is again a Brownian motion.
Non-example: A Poisson process starts at $0$ and has independent increments, but its paths jump and its increments are not normal.

steps: Take a Brownian motion $B$ and times $t_1<\dots<t_n$.
The increments $B_{t_i}-B_{t_{i-1}}$ are independent normal variables.
So $(B_{t_1},\dots,B_{t_n})$ is a linear image of a Gaussian vector, hence Gaussian.
The Brownian case adds continuous paths and the covariance $\operatorname{Cov}(B_s,B_t)=\min(s,t)$.
links.why: Lets you treat Brownian motion through its mean and covariance, as for any Gaussian process.

steps: Take a Brownian motion $B$ with its natural filtration $(\mathcal{F}_s)$.
For $s<t$, the increment $B_t-B_s$ is independent of $\mathcal{F}_s$ and has mean $0$.
So $E[B_t\mid\mathcal{F}_s]=B_s+E[B_t-B_s]=B_s$, and $B$ is a martingale.
The Brownian case adds continuous paths and normal increments.
links.why: Lets you use martingale theorems, such as optional sampling, for Brownian motion.

reminder: A C*-algebra is a complex Banach algebra with an involution that satisfies $\|x^*x\|=\|x\|^2$.
definition: A C*-algebra is a [Banach algebra](c:banach-algebra) $A$ over the [complex numbers](c:complex-number) with an [involution](c:involution) $x\mapsto x^*$ that satisfies the C*-identity $\|x^*x\|=\|x\|^2$ for all $x\in A$. Equivalently, it is a norm-closed algebra of bounded operators on a Hilbert space that contains the adjoint of each of its members.
examples: The field $\mathbb{C}$ with $z^*=\bar z$ and $\|z\|=|z|$ is a C*-algebra.
The matrix algebra $M_n(\mathbb{C})$ with the operator norm and the conjugate transpose is a C*-algebra.
The algebra $C(K)$ of continuous functions on a compact Hausdorff space $K$, with the supremum norm and $f^*=\bar f$, is a C*-algebra.
Non-example: The algebra $M_2(\mathbb{C})$ with the Hilbert-Schmidt norm is a Banach algebra with involution but is not a C*-algebra, because $\|I\|^2=2\ne\sqrt2=\|I^*I\|$.

steps: Take a C*-algebra $A$ with its norm and involution.
It is a complete normed algebra over $\mathbb{C}$, so it is a Banach algebra.
The C*-case adds the involution $x\mapsto x^*$ and the identity $\|x^*x\|=\|x\|^2$.
The identity ties the norm to the algebra: it forces $\|x^*\|=\|x\|$ and makes the norm unique.
links.why: Shows that a C*-algebra is a Banach algebra whose norm is determined by its algebra structure.

steps: Take a von Neumann algebra $M\subseteq B(H)$, a *-subalgebra of bounded operators that is closed in the weak operator topology.
The weak operator topology is coarser than the norm topology, so $M$ is also norm closed.
A norm-closed *-subalgebra of $B(H)$ is a C*-algebra.
So $M$ is a C*-algebra; the von Neumann case adds closure in the weak operator topology.
links.why: Shows that von Neumann algebras are C*-algebras with extra closure, so C*-theory applies to them.

reminder: A contour integral adds up a complex function along a path, weighted by the path's velocity $\gamma'(t)$.
definition: For a continuous [complex](c:complex-number) function $f$ and a piecewise [smooth curve](c:smooth-curve) $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb{C}$, the contour integral is $\int_\gamma f(z)\,dz=\int_a^bf(\gamma(t))\,\gamma'(t)\,dt$. The right side is an ordinary [integral](c:riemann-integral) of a complex-valued function of $t$.
examples: For the unit circle $\gamma(t)=e^{it}$ with $0\le t\le2\pi$, we get $\oint dz/z=2\pi i$.
For a closed curve $\gamma$ and $n\ge0$, we get $\int_\gamma z^n\,dz=0$.
For every curve $\gamma$, we get $\int_\gamma dz=\gamma(b)-\gamma(a)$.
Non-example: The arc-length integral $\int_\gamma f\,|dz|$ is not a contour integral, because it uses $|\gamma'(t)|$; on the unit circle it gives $2\pi$ for $f=1$, while $\oint dz=0$.

steps: Write $z=x+iy$ and $f=u+iv$ with real functions $u$ and $v$.
Multiplying out gives $f\,dz=(u\,dx-v\,dy)+i(v\,dx+u\,dy)$.
Each part is a real 1-form $P\,dx+Q\,dy$, and its line integral over $\gamma$ is defined.
So the contour integral equals $\int_\gamma(u\,dx-v\,dy)+i\int_\gamma(v\,dx+u\,dy)$, a sum of two real line integrals.
links.why: Lets you use line integral tools, such as Green's theorem, to prove results on contour integrals.

reminder: A holomorphic vector bundle is a complex vector bundle over a complex manifold whose transition functions are holomorphic.
definition: A holomorphic vector bundle of rank $r$ is a [complex vector bundle](c:complex-vector-bundle) $E\to X$ over a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) $X$ with a cover by [local trivializations](c:local-trivialization) $E|_{U_i}\cong U_i\times\mathbb{C}^r$ whose transition functions $g_{ij}:U_i\cap U_j\to GL_r(\mathbb{C})$ are [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function).
examples: The trivial bundle $X\times\mathbb{C}^r$ is a holomorphic vector bundle.
The holomorphic tangent bundle $T^{1,0}X$ of a complex manifold $X$ is a holomorphic vector bundle.
The tautological line bundle over $\mathbb{CP}^n$, whose fibre over a line $\ell$ is $\ell$ itself, is a holomorphic line bundle.
Non-example: On a complex torus, a smooth complex line bundle whose first Chern class is not of type $(1,1)$ has no holomorphic structure.

steps: Take a holomorphic vector bundle $E\to X$ with holomorphic transition functions $g_{ij}$.
Holomorphic maps are smooth, so the $g_{ij}$ are smooth and $E$ is a smooth complex vector bundle.
A holomorphic structure adds the condition that the $g_{ij}$ are holomorphic, not only smooth.
Not every complex vector bundle over a complex manifold admits such a structure.
links.why: Shows that holomorphic bundles are complex bundles with extra structure, so topological invariants such as Chern classes apply.

reminder: An $L^p$ space is the space of measurable functions whose $p$th power is integrable, with functions equal almost everywhere identified.
definition: For a measure space $(X,\mu)$ and $1\le p<\infty$, the space $L^p(\mu)$ is the set of [measurable functions](c:measurable-function) $f$ with $\int|f|^p\,d\mu<\infty$, in the sense of the [Lebesgue integral](c:lebesgue-integral), where functions equal [almost everywhere](c:almost-everywhere) count as one element. Its [norm](c:norm) is $\|f\|_p=\left(\int|f|^p\,d\mu\right)^{1/p}$. For $p=\infty$, the norm is the [essential supremum](c:essential-supremum) of $|f|$.
examples: The space $L^2[0,1]$ is the space of square-integrable functions on $[0,1]$.
For counting measure on $\mathbb{N}$, the space $L^p$ is the sequence space $\ell^p$.
The function $x^{-1/3}$ on $(0,1]$ lies in $L^2$ but not in $L^3$.
Non-example: The function $1/x$ on $(0,1)$ is not in $L^1$, because $\int_0^1x^{-1}\,dx=\infty$.

steps: Take $L^p(\mu)$ with $1\le p\le\infty$.
Minkowski's inequality gives the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_p$, so $L^p$ is a normed space.
Identification of functions equal almost everywhere makes $\|f\|_p=0$ force $f=0$.
The Riesz-Fischer theorem shows that every Cauchy sequence converges, so $L^p$ is complete and is a Banach space.
links.why: Lets you use Banach space tools, such as the Hahn-Banach theorem, in every $L^p$ space.

reminder: A Noetherian ring is a ring in which every ascending chain of ideals becomes constant.
definition: A [ring](c:ring) $R$ is Noetherian when it satisfies the [ascending chain condition](c:ascending-chain-condition) on [ideals](c:ideal): every chain $I_1\subseteq I_2\subseteq\cdots$ of ideals is constant from some index on. Equivalently, every ideal of $R$ is finitely generated.
examples: Every field and the ring $\mathbb{Z}$ are Noetherian.
The polynomial ring $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ over a field $k$ is Noetherian, by Hilbert's basis theorem.
Non-example: The polynomial ring $k[x_1,x_2,\dots]$ in infinitely many variables is not Noetherian, because the chain $(x_1)\subset(x_1,x_2)\subset\cdots$ never becomes constant.

steps: Regard the ring $R$ as a module over itself.
Its submodules are exactly the ideals of $R$.
A module is Noetherian when every ascending chain of submodules stabilizes.
So $R$ is a Noetherian ring exactly when $R$ is a Noetherian $R$-module.
links.why: Lets you use the module theory of Noetherian modules, such as stability under submodules and quotients, for rings.

steps: Take a principal ideal domain $R$ and an ascending chain of ideals $I_1\subseteq I_2\subseteq\cdots$.
The union $I=\bigcup_kI_k$ is an ideal, so $I=(a)$ for one element $a$.
The element $a$ lies in some $I_k$, so $I=(a)\subseteq I_k\subseteq I$ and the chain is constant from $k$ on.
So $R$ is Noetherian; a Noetherian ring may have ideals that need several generators, such as $(x,y)$ in $k[x,y]$.
links.why: Shows that every principal ideal domain is Noetherian, so $\mathbb{Z}$ and $k[x]$ are examples.

reminder: The normal distribution has a bell-shaped density and is determined by its mean and variance.
definition: The normal distribution $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, with $\mu\in\mathbb{R}$ and $\sigma>0$, is the [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) on $\mathbb{R}$ with [density](c:probability-density-function) $\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(2\sigma^2)}$. Its [expected value](c:expected-value) is $\mu$ and its [variance](c:variance) is $\sigma^2$.
examples: The standard normal distribution $N(0,1)$ has the density $e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$.
A sum of independent normal random variables is normal, and the means and variances add.
Non-example: The Cauchy distribution has a bell-shaped density $1/(\pi(1+x^2))$ but has no mean and no variance, so it is not normal.

steps: Take the law $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ on $\mathbb{R}$.
Every linear functional of $\mathbb{R}$ has the form $x\mapsto cx$.
The image of $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ under it is $N(c\mu,c^2\sigma^2)$, which is again normal.
So $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ is a Gaussian measure on $\mathbb{R}$; Gaussian measures also cover higher dimensions and point masses.
links.why: Shows the normal distribution as the one-dimensional Gaussian measure, which leads to Gaussian vectors and processes.

reminder: Random variables converge in distribution when their distribution functions converge at every continuity point of the limit.
definition: Real [random variables](c:random-variable) $X_n$ converge in distribution to $X$ when $F_{X_n}(x)\to F_X(x)$ at every point $x$ where the [distribution function](c:distribution-function) $F_X$ is continuous. This depends only on the laws of the variables, not on the probability space.
examples: By the central limit theorem, standardized sums of independent identically distributed variables with finite variance converge in distribution to $N(0,1)$.
The constants $X_n=1/n$ converge in distribution to $0$, although $F_{X_n}(0)=0$ does not tend to $F_X(0)=1$: the point $0$ is a jump, so the definition ignores it.
Non-example: The constants $X_n=n$ do not converge in distribution, because $F_{X_n}(x)\to0$ for every $x$, and the limit $0$ is not a distribution function.

steps: Take $X_n\to X$ in probability and a continuity point $x$ of $F_X$.
For $\varepsilon>0$, we get $F_{X_n}(x)\le F_X(x+\varepsilon)+P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)$.
In the same way, $F_{X_n}(x)\ge F_X(x-\varepsilon)-P(|X_n-X|>\varepsilon)$.
Let $n\to\infty$ and then $\varepsilon\to0$; continuity of $F_X$ at $x$ gives $F_{X_n}(x)\to F_X(x)$.
links.why: Shows that convergence in probability implies convergence in distribution, which is the weaker notion.

reminder: A cyclic group is a group in which one element generates every element as a power.
definition: A [group](c:group) $G$ is cyclic when some element $g$ generates it: every element of $G$ equals $g^k$ for some integer $k$, so $G=\langle g\rangle$. Every cyclic group is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}$ or to $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$.
examples: The group $(\mathbb{Z},+)$ is cyclic, generated by $1$.
The group $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ is cyclic, generated by the class of $1$.
The $n$th roots of unity in $\mathbb{C}^\times$ form a cyclic group, generated by $e^{2\pi i/n}$.
Non-example: The Klein four-group $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ is not cyclic, because every element has order at most $2$ and no element generates all four.

steps: Take a cyclic group $G=\langle g\rangle$ and two elements $g^a$ and $g^b$.
The product rule for powers gives $g^ag^b=g^{a+b}=g^bg^a$.
So the product is commutative, and $G$ is abelian.
The cyclic case adds that one element generates the whole group; $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ is abelian but not cyclic.
links.why: Shows that every cyclic group is abelian, so you can use commutativity there.

reminder: An elliptic curve is a smooth projective curve of genus one with a chosen rational point.
definition: An elliptic curve over a field $K$ is a smooth projective [algebraic curve](c:algebraic-curve) of genus one with a chosen $K$-[rational point](c:rational-point) $O$. When $\operatorname{char}K\ne2,3$, it has an equation $y^2=x^3+ax+b$ with $4a^3+27b^2\ne0$ and $O$ at infinity, and its points form an [abelian group](c:abelian-group) with identity $O$.
examples: The curve $y^2=x^3-x$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ is an elliptic curve, because $4a^3+27b^2=-4\ne0$.
The curve $y^2=x^3+1$ is an elliptic curve, because $4a^3+27b^2=27\ne0$.
Over $\mathbb{C}$, every complex torus $\mathbb{C}/\Lambda$ with a lattice $\Lambda$ is an elliptic curve.
Non-example: The curve $y^2=x^3$ is not an elliptic curve, because it has a cusp at $(0,0)$; here $4a^3+27b^2=0$.

steps: Take an elliptic curve $E$ over $K$.
Its smooth projective model is a one-dimensional variety, so $E$ is an algebraic curve.
The elliptic case adds the condition that the genus is one.
It also adds the rational point $O$, which becomes the identity of the group law.
links.why: Lets you use the theory of algebraic curves, such as the Riemann-Roch theorem, for elliptic curves.

steps: Take an elliptic curve $E$ with base point $O$.
Chord-and-tangent addition makes the points of $E$ an abelian group, and addition $E\times E\to E$ is a morphism.
So $E$ is a smooth projective variety with a group law given by morphisms, which is an abelian variety.
Its dimension is one, so elliptic curves are exactly the one-dimensional abelian varieties.
links.why: Shows that elliptic curves are the simplest abelian varieties, so higher-dimensional theory generalizes them.

reminder: The expected value of a random variable is its probability-weighted average, the integral of the variable against the probability measure.
definition: The expected value of an integrable [random variable](c:random-variable) $X$ on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)$ is $E[X]=\int_\Omega X\,dP$, the [Lebesgue integral](c:lebesgue-integral) of $X$ against the [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $P$. For a discrete variable, $E[X]=\sum_xx\,P(X=x)$.
examples: A fair die has $E[X]=(1+2+\cdots+6)/6=3.5$.
For an event $A$, the indicator has $E[1_A]=P(A)$.
A Bernoulli variable with $P(X=1)=p$ and $P(X=0)=1-p$ has $E[X]=p$.
Non-example: A Cauchy random variable has no expected value, because $\int|x|\,dx/(\pi(1+x^2))=\infty$.

steps: Take a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)$ and a random variable $X$.
The Lebesgue integral $\int X\,dP$ is defined for measurable $X$ with $\int|X|\,dP<\infty$.
The expected value is this integral for the special measure $P$ with $P(\Omega)=1$.
So linearity and monotonicity of the integral hold for $E$.
links.why: Lets you use the convergence theorems of the Lebesgue integral, such as dominated convergence, for expected values.

reminder: A group action assigns to each group element a transformation of a set, compatible with the group product and identity.
definition: An action of a [group](c:group) $G$ on a [set](c:set) $X$ is a map $G\times X\to X$, written $(g,x)\mapsto g\cdot x$, with $e\cdot x=x$ and $(gh)\cdot x=g\cdot(h\cdot x)$ for all $g,h\in G$ and $x\in X$.
examples: The symmetric group $S_n$ acts on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ by $\sigma\cdot i=\sigma(i)$.
The group $GL_n(\mathbb{R})$ acts on $\mathbb{R}^n$ by matrix multiplication.
Every group acts on itself by left multiplication and by conjugation.
Non-example: For a nonabelian group, the rule $g\cdot x=xg$ is not a left action, because $(gh)\cdot x=xgh$ differs from $g\cdot(h\cdot x)=xhg$ in general.

steps: Take a transitive action of $G$ on $X$.
It is an action, because the same map $G\times X\to X$ satisfies both axioms.
Transitivity adds that for all $x,y\in X$ some $g$ has $g\cdot x=y$.
Then $X$ is in bijection with the coset space $G/\operatorname{Stab}(x)$.
links.why: Shows that every transitive action is a quotient of the group, so a general action splits into transitive pieces, the orbits.

steps: Take a representation $\rho:G\to GL(V)$ on a vector space $V$.
Define the action of $g$ on $v$ by $g\cdot v=\rho(g)v$.
Then $e\cdot v=v$ and $(gh)\cdot v=\rho(g)\rho(h)v=g\cdot(h\cdot v)$.
So a representation is an action on a vector space by linear maps; the representation adds linearity.
links.why: Shows that representations are group actions that respect linear structure, so action tools such as orbits apply.
